newsitem.title: USA: Russian "Godfather" given 115 months in U.S. prison.
newsitem.headline: Russian "Godfather" given 115 months in U.S. prison.

text.p: A U.S. federal judge on Wednesday sentenced the reputed "Godfather" of Russian organised crime in the United States, who was convicted of extortion and marriage fraud, to 115 months in prison.

Vyacheslav Ivankov, 56, the man federal authorites call one of the most powerful Russian mobsters in America, was convicted in July with three other Russians of conspiracy and attempting to extort $3.5 million from a Russian emigre investment firm.

Swearing his innocence and proclaiming himself the real victim, Ivankov said,"I'm not in church, I have no need to make a confession. The crime has not been committed by us, but the crime has been committed against us."
"They have been staging this cheap farce to reap these laurel leaves, and all at our misfortune," Ivankov said through a translator.

He was also convicted in a separate trial of fraudulently marrying an American woman in order to obtain a resident alien card which would have allowed him to work in this country. Ivankov had faced up to 40 years on the two charges.
He will receive credit for the 19 months served in a federal correctional facilty since he was arrested.
Of his three co-defendants, Valery Novak, 46, was sentenced to 51 months; Vladimir Topko, 35, was sentenced to 54 months, and Sergei Ilgner, 33, was sentenced to 67 months.

Handing down Ivankov's sentence, U.S. District Judge Carol Amon said her decision was "based on the jury's verdict and the evidence I heard in this courtroom," rather than on any media reports as Ivankov charged during the almost two hours he spent pleading for mercy.
She also said her decision was not based "on any criminal conduct Ivankov is alleged to have done in the Soviet Union."

Presenting what he called his "corrected views" of the case, Ivankov said it was nothing more than a "flow of lies against me." He blasted the Russian unit of the FBI for spreading distortion, gossip and lies about him, and also accused the government of acting in a "biased manner."

The case against Ivankov and the three others came about after extortion attempts were made against two Russian businessmen who ran a small Wall Street investment firm, Summit International. When the two balked at paying, the defendants forced the victims to sign a contract agreeing to pay $3.5 million to one of Ivankov's criminal associates, prosecutors said.
A father of one of the two men was fatally beaten on a Moscow train platform in April, 1995.

Ivankov was born in Russia in 1940 and was eventually sentenced to 10 years in a Siberian prison in 1982 for participating in the thefts of homes of wealthy Russians. He bribed a judge in 1991 and escaped to the United States with a faked exit visa, according to the extortion charges.

In recent years, U.S. officials have expressed fear that criminals from the former Soviet Union have successfully expanded their operations into North America since the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.
The Russian mob's activities have included money laundering, fraud, drug dealing and murder.

Since his arrival in the United States, Ivankov was based in Brighton Beach, in Brooklyn, which has become the centre of the Russian emigre community in the United States and an alleged nexus of the Russian mob's criminal activity.
